name: Bruxism night guard

lead: A bruxism night guard, or occlusal splint, is a hard or soft plastic appliance worn over the teeth during sleep. People wear one to keep grinding and clenching from flattening and chipping their teeth, and to ease jaw strain.

The guard puts a plastic barrier between upper and lower teeth so grinding forces wear the appliance instead of the enamel. Long-term grinding can flatten, chip or wear teeth and change how the smile looks. Splints are described as a first-line protective measure, and systematic reviews note the evidence is limited and that the guard does not stop the underlying muscle activity.

paras: Dentists make custom guards from impressions or scans; stock and boil-and-bite versions are sold over the counter. It is worn every night, and users often pair it with stress and sleep changes.

Splints are widely used and generally safe, but reviews find little direct evidence that they reduce tooth wear or cure bruxism. Some designs may increase clenching or cause bite changes with full-time use, and ill-fitting stock guards can be uncomfortable. A dentist can check for sleep apnea and other drivers.

chain: Less tooth wear and jaw strain
angle.text: Users wear night guards to stop grinding from flattening and chipping their teeth and to ease jaw strain, which they link to keeping the smile and jaw intact. The guard protects teeth; effects on facial appearance are untested.

lead: A bruxism night guard, also called an occlusal splint, bite guard or nightguard, is a removable hard or soft plastic appliance worn over the teeth, usually at night, intended to protect them from the effects of grinding and clenching. Dentists make custom versions from impressions or scans, while stock and boil-and-bite versions are sold over the counter. [1][2]

Bruxism is defined in Grokipedia, citing a 2024 international consensus, as repetitive jaw-muscle activity involving clenching, grinding, or bracing of the mandible during sleep or wakefulness, and the consensus is described as treating it as a behaviour on a continuum rather than a disorder unless it causes harm such as dental damage or pain. [1] Occlusal splints and mouthguards are described there as a first-line measure to protect teeth. [1] The appearance case for a night guard is that long-term grinding can flatten, chip or wear teeth and shorten or change the look of the smile, so a guard is worn to keep tooth length, edges and restorations such as veneers, crowns and bonding intact. [1][3]

Researchers have examined whether splints reduce bruxism itself, protect against wear or help temporomandibular symptoms. Systematic reviews of occlusal splints for bruxism and for temporomandibular disorder have been published, with authors generally noting that the quality and amount of evidence is limited and that the appliance is a protective device that does not remove the underlying muscle activity. [4][5][6][2] Wear of splint materials has been the subject of its own systematic review. [7]

Wikipedia reports a 2024 meta-analysis putting global bruxism prevalence at about 22 percent, and states that splints mainly protect teeth from wear rather than stopping the grinding. [3] A 2023 systematic review of 15 studies concluded that splint therapy is a viable approach for sleep bruxism with the choice individualised, while a 2020 systematic review of 37 trials found very low certainty evidence overall; the two reviews are summarised under Clinical studies. [6][5]

paras: A night guard places a layer of plastic between the upper and lower teeth so that the forces of grinding and clenching fall on the appliance. Reviews distinguish several types of occlusal splints used for bruxism and temporomandibular disorders, including stabilisation splints and soft appliances, and compare their use. [6][2][5] Custom guards are fabricated by dentists or laboratories, while over-the-counter products are generic or heat-moulded by the wearer.

A systematic review of the wear behaviour of occlusal splint materials made by different manufacturing methods covered in vitro and in vivo testing of splints and the teeth opposing them, using materials such as polymethyl methacrylate. [7] The term night guard is also used for the trays worn for overnight tooth bleaching, which is a separate use of similar appliances. [8][9]

According to Grokipedia, sleep bruxism is thought to affect about 8 to 10 percent of adults and awake bruxism a larger share, with estimates varying by assessment method; it is considered multifactorial, with stress, sleep-related factors such as obstructive sleep apnea, medications and lifestyle all discussed as contributors. Symptoms listed include jaw muscle soreness, morning headaches, tooth sensitivity and audible grinding, and in severe cases flattened or chipped teeth, gum recession and temporomandibular joint problems. [1] That source also lists botulinum toxin injections into the masseter, behavioural therapy and treatment of underlying sleep disorders as other management approaches. [1] Because Grokipedia is AI-generated, these figures are given as a general orientation rather than as established statistics.

Bruxism is also discussed in implant dentistry, where it has traditionally been regarded as a risk factor, although a review found no consistent proof that bruxism causes implant overload and recommended a careful approach, and a polysomnography study examined sleep bruxism in patients with implants. [10][11]

Bruxism is excessive grinding or clenching of the teeth that is not part of normal chewing or speaking. It is divided into sleep bruxism, which occurs during sleep and is often noticed by a partner through grinding sounds, and awake bruxism, which is usually clenching during concentration or stress. The two forms probably have different causes. [3] A 2024 meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia puts overall prevalence at around 22 percent, with sleep and awake forms each at roughly 21 to 23 percent, and adult sleep bruxism is often quoted at around 8 percent. [3]

Causes are considered multifactorial. Sleep bruxism is linked to arousals during sleep and central nervous system mechanisms; awake bruxism to stress, anxiety and habits such as nail or cheek biting. Smoking, caffeine, alcohol and certain stimulants and medications are reported associations, and the bite itself, once thought the main driver, is now thought to play little or no role. [3]

sections.h: Effects on teeth and facial appearance
paras: Frequent grinding can flatten and wear the chewing surfaces of teeth, chip or fracture them, and cause failure of fillings and crowns, which are the most common reasons the condition is first noticed. [3] It can also enlarge the masseter muscles, the thick jaw muscles at the angle of the jaw, giving a wider, squarer lower face, together with muscle tenderness, jaw pain, headaches and joint clicking. [3]

This is why night guards appear in appearance discussions: protecting enamel preserves tooth length and shape, and masseter enlargement is a recognised sign of bruxism. A guard is aimed at tooth protection rather than muscle size; masseter botulinum toxin injections are a separate treatment that dentists also use for severe bruxism. [3]

Occlusal splints are plastic devices, usually acrylic, covering some or all teeth and worn mostly at night. They can be hard or soft, full or partial coverage, and lower splints are often better tolerated. [3] Wikipedia says they protect teeth from wear but do not stop the grinding itself, are probably ineffective for awake bruxism because they are worn during sleep, and that in a minority of people they may worsen grinding. [3]

Devices that cover only the front teeth, such as NTI-TSS, are designed for nighttime use and can shift tooth positions with long-term wear. Mandibular advancement devices made for sleep apnoea may reduce sleep bruxism but can cause discomfort. A guard with worn-through holes no longer protects the teeth and needs replacing. [3] Repositioning splints designed to change the bite have shown no advantage over other therapies in randomised trials. [3]

The grinding of teeth appears in ancient Chinese texts, and a 610 CE treatise linked clenching during sleep with qi deficiency and blood stasis. The French term 'bruxomanie' was proposed in 1907, and Bertrand Frohman coined 'bruxism' in 1931. In the 1960s Sigurd Ramfjord promoted the view that bite problems caused bruxism, which most researchers now replace with a biopsychosocial model. [3]
Wikipedia adds that occlusal adjustment, grinding down teeth to alter the bite, is contested, and that repositioning splints intended to change the bite showed no advantage in randomised trials. [3]

sections.h: Appearance relevance: teeth, smile and jaw
paras: Tooth wear is the visible consequence that interests people concerned with their looks. Wikipedia lists attrition, fractures, failed fillings and crowns and hypersensitivity among the dental signs of bruxism, and notes that dental restorations in people who grind often fail, so dentists are described as keeping restorations simple and making crowns and veneers extra durable. [3] Protective guards are therefore commonly prescribed alongside cosmetic work such as veneers.

Masseter hypertrophy, an enlarged jaw muscle, is another recognised sign. [3] In appearance communities a broad, square lower face is sometimes attributed to clenching; a splint does not target the muscle, whereas botulinum toxin injected into the masseter is used for severe bruxism, and a 2020 overview of systematic reviews summarised by Wikipedia reported reductions in pain and sleep-bruxism frequency at 6 and 12 months compared with placebo or conventional treatment, with effects lasting around three months. [3]

The NHS describes the signs as jaw pain, worn or broken teeth, tooth sensitivity and headaches, says that treatment is not always needed, and describes a dentist-fitted night-time mouth guard as one option to protect the teeth alongside stress reduction, sleep habits and cutting back on smoking, alcohol and caffeine. [12]

A 2020 systematic review of oral splints compared with no or minimal treatment included 37 randomised trials, 34 of them on temporomandibular disorder, two on bruxism and one on both. For TMD pain at 0 to 3 months, 13 trials with 1,076 participants showed no significant pain reduction with splints. No trial measured tooth wear in bruxism, one trial of 78 patients reported short-term pain reduction, and the authors rated the certainty of evidence as very low and called for better-designed trials. The review found no evidence that splints caused adverse events, though adverse events were poorly reported. [5][5]

A 2023 systematic review of occlusal splints for sleep bruxism included 15 studies with 529 participants, mostly randomised trials in young adults. Biofeedback splints and adjustable splints reduced bruxism episodes in individual trials, rigid splints generally reduced muscle activity, soft splints gave mixed results with one study reporting increased activity in some participants, and soft splints reduced muscle and joint pain in children. The authors concluded that splint therapy is a viable approach whose choice should be individualised, noting heterogeneous splint types, short follow-up and small samples. [6]

A 2021 systematic review examined the efficacy of occlusal splints in bruxism, and a 2023 review described splint types and their effectiveness in TMD management. [4][2] Reviews in this area commonly note small trials, short follow-up and variable outcome measures, which limits conclusions about tooth wear or bruxism activity itself.

Other trials have used night guards for related purposes: a controlled clinical trial applied a night guard to sleep-related dry mouth, and a randomized trial compared a betaine mouthwash with an intraoral device for dry mouth. [13][14] A 1992 double-blind controlled study and later trials used night guards to deliver 10 percent carbamide peroxide whitening gel. [8][9]

Splints are widely prescribed and reported as generally well tolerated, though a review noted that adverse events are poorly reported. [5] Wikipedia states that in a minority of people splints may worsen sleep bruxism, that front-tooth-only devices can shift tooth positions with long-term wear, and that a guard worn through needs replacing. [3] Poorly fitting or stock guards may be uncomfortable, and splints do not address underlying contributors such as sleep apnea or stress, for which clinical assessment is used. [1] The wear of the appliance and its effect on opposing teeth has been studied in materials research. [7]

sections.h: Use in appearance and grooming discussions
paras: Night guards are typically discussed in dental-aesthetics and jaw-appearance conversations as protection for tooth length and restorations rather than as a facial change, and are often mentioned next to masseter botulinum toxin, jaw exercisers and veneers. Custom guards are made by dentists from impressions or scans, while boil-and-bite and stock guards are sold over the counter at lower prices. [1][2]

A 2021 New York Times article, shared on Hacker News, was titled "Grind Your Teeth? Your Night Guard May Not Be the Right Fix", reflecting mainstream coverage of the question of whether guards address grinding. [15] Dentists' own wording, as above, is that guards protect teeth rather than stop grinding. [3]

lore.intro: Night guards are mentioned in appearance communities mostly as a way to protect teeth and cosmetic dental work, alongside discussion of jaw clenching and masseter size; dentists' and reviewers' positions are summarised below.
